title: The smaller plate
setting: A doctor talks to a patient who has tried three diets.

lines.t: I've tried three diets in two years. None of them lasted.
What do you actually eat on a normal Tuesday?
Nothing terrible. Bread, chicken, rice, a takeaway on Friday.
That sounds fine. How much of it?
A full plate. It's always been a full plate.
Then it's portion size, not the food. Nothing needs to be banned.
So what do I change?
Use a smaller plate, and stop eating in front of the television.
That's it?
It's boring, and boring is what people can still do in March.

title: Look at the plate
setting: Somebody eats the right food and nothing changes.

lines.t: I eat well. I don't understand why nothing changes.
Tell me what was on the plate last night.
Chicken, rice, salad. That's a balanced diet, isn't it?
It is. How much rice?
Two thirds of the plate.
Then the food is right and the portion size is doing the damage.
So now I have to weigh everything.
For two weeks, and then you'll know what 80 grams looks like. Portion control is a skill and it takes a fortnight.
That's manageable.
And drink water with every meal. Most people who stay hydrated eat less without trying to.

title: Counting the wrong thing
setting: Three months of counting calories and constant tiredness.

lines.t: I've counted every calorie for three months.
And?
I'm tired all the time.
A calorie tells you about energy. It says nothing about the nutrients.
Meaning?
Nine hundred calories of biscuits and nine hundred of fish do different things to you.
How much protein should I be having?
Roughly your weight in grams if you're training. Carbohydrate isn't the enemy either, it's what your legs run on.
And fat?
Limit the saturated fat. Your body needs the rest.
Should I take a supplement?
Vitamin D in winter, in this country, yes. The rest you'd get from food, and fibre is the one almost everybody is short of.

title: Tuesday is the hard one
setting: Six days of the week are fine and one is not.

lines.t: Monday and Sunday are fine. Tuesday I get home at eight.
And what happens at eight?
A ready meal, or we order a takeaway.
How often do you eat out as well?
Twice a week, maybe.
So four meals a week are outside your control, and you're judging yourself on the other seventeen.
Then Tuesday is the problem.
Tuesday is the one to solve. Cook something home-cooked on Sunday that reheats well.
My husband won't eat anything plant-based.
Then don't call it that. Put lentils into something he already likes.
And the bread?
Wholegrain where you can. Processed food isn't forbidden, it's simply most of what's in the cupboard right now.

title: It isn't a preference
setting: Ordering in a restaurant, and being taken seriously.

lines.t: Is the soup dairy-free?
I'll check with the kitchen.
Thank you. I'm lactose intolerant, so a little cream matters.
Is that an allergy or a preference?
Somewhere between. It won't send me to hospital, and the evening is over.
Understood. I'll treat it the same way I'd treat an allergy.
That's the right answer, and not everybody gives it.
My sister is gluten-free. I've heard what people say to her.
'A little bit won't hurt.'
Every single time. I'll bring the list of what the kitchen can actually do.

title: Reading the label
setting: A nutritionist shows a class how to read packaging.

lines.t: It says low-fat and high in protein. That's healthy, isn't it?
Guess the sugar content. One small pot.
Maybe six grams?
Twenty-one. More than a standard chocolate bar.
But the front says nothing about that.
The front is advertising. The back is information.
What should I actually look at?
Per hundred grams: sugar, saturated fat, salt. Three lines.
And the ingredients?
Listed by quantity. If sugar is in the first three, you know what you're buying.

title: The low-fat yoghurt
setting: The healthy-looking product turns out to be something else.

lines.t: I bought the low-fat yoghurt, like you said.
Turn it over and read the food label.
Sugar, 14 grams.
In 100 grams of yoghurt. That's most of a child's recommended daily amount.
But it's low-fat.
Take the fat out and something has to make it taste of something.
So the sugar content is what I should be reading.
Added sugar especially. Fruit brings its own, and that's a different thing.
How do I tell them apart?
The ingredients list. If sugar appears in the first three, put it back on the shelf.
I'll write a shopping list and stop deciding in the shop.

title: Cut out or cut down
setting: Eleven days without sugar and a familiar ending approaching.

lines.t: I've cut out sugar completely. Eleven days.
How do you feel?
Furious.
Which is why it won't last. What happened the last time?
Nine days, then a whole cake.
Then cut down on it instead. Sugar in your coffee, fine. A dessert on Saturday, fine.
That feels like failing.
A sustainable habit is one you'll still have in March. Eleven furious days is something else.
So everything in moderation.
Everything except the things you genuinely can't stop at one of. Those you leave in the shop.
And the meal prep?
Sunday, two hours, four lunches. A treat stops being dangerous once there's food in the fridge.

title: Nothing until four
setting: A day with no lunch and a difficult evening.

lines.t: Talk me through yesterday.
Coffee at seven. Then nothing until four.
So you skipped two meals.
I wasn't hungry. My appetite has been strange lately.
And at four?
Everything in the kitchen.
That's what happens. Skip a meal and the body collects the difference with interest.
I know I overeat in the evening.
Is it hunger, or is it the end of the day?
The end of the day, mostly. It's comfort eating and I know it while I'm doing it.
Then eat a proper lunch, keep a snack in your bag, and when you crave something at nine, sit down and eat it at the table.
Mindful eating, you mean.
Slowly, without a screen. Half of it disappears while you're looking at your phone and your body never registers it.

title: Four kilos, four times
setting: The same four kilos, lost and found, four years running.

lines.t: I've lost four kilos four times.
And put on weight in between each one.
Every time.
That's yo-yo dieting, and it's harder on you than the four kilos ever were.
The last one was a fad diet. Six weeks, no bread.
And what happened in week seven?
Bread.
You already know how to lose weight. You've done it four times.
Keeping it off is the part I've never managed.
Which has a slower, duller answer. Watch what you eat, without a rule that ends in April.
Nobody sells that in a book.
Nobody can. It's the same twelve sentences every time, and they're free.

title: Slow metabolism
setting: The most popular explanation in the world, examined.

lines.t: My problem is a slow metabolism. It runs in the family.
Possibly. It's also the most popular explanation in the world.
You don't believe me.
I believe metabolism varies. Between two people your size, the difference is smaller than one pastry a day.
That's depressing.
It's good news, because a pastry is something you can change.
I get very tired after lunch.
What's in the lunch?
Bread, usually. A sandwich.

Then your blood sugar climbs and drops and the afternoon happens. Add protein, add fibre, and give your gut health a month of that before you decide anything. Food takes time to digest and habits take longer.
